intro.caption: Lesson 7-2 — rational numbers and their opposites on the number line. The Delvers keep a ledger of every gold bar they win or lose. Tonight, the numbers in it look strange. Three reader gates and a boss ledger stand between them and the truth.

balloons.t: Someone wrote in our ledger. Now it says −¾, 1¼, −0.5… fractions and decimals!
Gains are positive. Losses are negative. Every entry has ONE exact spot on the number line.
−¾ has a 4 in it. So it goes way out at −4. I'll stand there!
The 4 tells how many equal parts. It does not tell where to stand.

pages.caption: Kwame used the denominator as a spot. Choose the right tool first: find the two integers the number sits between, then cut that space into equal parts.

balloons.t: Step 1: which two integers? Step 2: cut that gap into equal parts. Step 3: count.
Every gain has a matching loss. Same size. Other side of 0.
Opposites! Like a mirror, with 0 in the middle.
This page says −0.75. That page says −¾. Are they two entries?
From inside this net, I say: same spot, different clothes.
You owe ME. Unless you can read my ledger better.
Every entry in its exact spot. Even the sneaky ones.

win.caption: A rational number has one exact spot on the number line. Find the two integers it is between, cut that gap into as many equal parts as the denominator says, and count. Negatives go left of 0. Opposites are the same distance from 0 on different sides.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Place the Numbers
gates.badge: Line Rod — Fractions and Decimals on the Line
gates.prompt: Sol's rod marks every quarter between the integers. Place two ledger entries on two short stretches of the rod.
hints: Conceptual: the denominator tells how many equal parts each whole is cut into. It does not tell where the number goes.
Procedural: find the two integers the number sits between. Cut that gap into equal parts. Count from the integer closer to 0.

steps: The ½ means cut that gap into 2 equal parts. The dot goes halfway between −1 and −2.

items.q: The first entry is a loss of −¾ of a gold bar. Mark −¾.

fb.msg: That's −¼, only one quarter. The 4 cuts the gap into 4 parts. Count 3 of them left of 0.
That's −1, a whole step. −¾ stops after 3 of the 4 quarters.
That's +¾. The minus sign puts −¾ to the LEFT of 0.
That's −½, two quarters. Count one more quarter to the left.

items.fbDefault: −¾ is between 0 and −1. Cut that gap into 4 parts and count 3 to the left.

items.q: The next entry is −1.25. Mark it.

fb.msg: You counted ¼ from −2. Start at −1 and go one quarter MORE to the left.
You dropped the whole 1. −1.25 is past −1.
That's −1.5, halfway. 0.25 is only one quarter past −1.

items.fbDefault: −1.25 is between −1 and −2. Start at −1 and count one quarter to the left.

gates.pass: Two dots, two exact spots: −¾ just left of 0 and −1.25 just past −1. Sol cuts Kwame out of the net.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Mirror Entries
gates.prompt: Each gain in the ledger has a matching loss: its opposite.
hints: Conceptual: opposites are the same distance from 0, on different sides. The fraction part stays the same; only the side changes.
Procedural: count how many equal parts the number is from 0. Count the same number of parts on the other side.

steps: 2½ units right of 0 is 2.5. So the opposite of −2.5 is 2.5.

items.q: Anya found a gain of 1½ bars. Mark its matching loss: the opposite of 1½.

fb.msg: That's 1½ itself. Its opposite is on the other side of 0.
You dropped the whole 1. 1½ is one and a half units from 0, so its opposite is too.
Left side is right, but count again: 1½ is 3 halves from 0, not 2.

items.fbDefault: 1½ is 1½ units right of 0. Go 1½ units left of 0.

items.q: Which pair of ledger entries are opposites?

options.fb: Those are the SAME number written two ways. Opposites sit on different sides of 0.
4 is much farther from 0 than ¼. Opposites are the same distance from 0.
Both are left of 0. Opposites sit on different sides of 0.

gates.pass: Gain 1½, loss −1½. −0.5 and ½ sit the same distance from 0, like a mirror. The ledger glows a little.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Same Spot, New Clothes
gates.prompt: Bao checks if two entries are really one number written two ways.
hints: Conceptual: a fraction and a decimal that are equivalent sit at the exact same point on the line.
Procedural: change the fraction to a decimal by dividing the top by the bottom. Keep the sign.

steps: Both are negative, so −0.5 and −½ are the same point.
worked.q: Which fraction is the same point as −0.25?

items.q: Which entry lands on the same spot as −0.75?

options.fb: You read the digits 3 and 4 as a decimal. ¾ = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75.
That's flipped. −4/3 is past −1, so it is farther left than −0.75.
The minus sign is missing. 0.75 is the OPPOSITE of −0.75.

items.q: A smudged entry says −2⅓. Between which two integers is it?

options.fb: −2⅓ is past −2, farther from 0. It is not between −2 and −1.
The minus sign puts it left of 0, between two negative integers.
−2⅓ is only a little past −2. It has not reached −3.

gates.pass: −0.75 and −¾ are one entry, not two. −2⅓ sits between −3 and −2. Bao crosses out Grimble's extra line.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Grimble's Ledger
gates.prompt: Grimble's copy of the ledger has three locks. Read each entry at its exact spot.
hints: Conceptual: every rational number has one point. Negative numbers sit left of 0, and the more negative, the farther left.
Procedural: for each number, find the two integers around it first, then count the equal parts.

steps: 0.75 is 3 quarters, so count 3 quarters left from −2.

items.q: Lock 1 · Grimble's last entry is a loss of −1¾ bars. Mark it.

fb.msg: You dropped the whole 1. −1¾ is past −1.
That's only ¼ past −1. ¾ means 3 quarters past −1.
That's −1½, two quarters past −1. ¾ is three quarters past −1.

items.fbDefault: Find −1 and −2. Count 3 quarters left from −1.

items.q: Lock 2 · Grimble says −¾ belongs right next to −4 "because of the 4." Is he right?

options.t: Yes, the 4 tells where it goes
options.fb: That's Kwame's trap. The 4 tells how many equal parts make a whole.
−3 is three whole steps from 0. −¾ is less than one step.

items.q: Lock 3 · Grimble's fourth entry is a gain of ½ bar. Mark it.

fb.msg: That is −½, the opposite. A gain sits to the right of 0.
That is ¼. ½ is two quarters from 0.

items.fbDefault: Find 0, then count two quarters to the right.

gates.pass: CLICK, CLICK, CLICK. The ledger is read right: −1¾, −¾ beside 0, and −1.25, −¾, 0.25, ½ in order. Grimble owes THEM two gold bars.

journal.heading: Lesson 7-2 — what the ledger taught us
rows: Every rational number, fraction or decimal, has one point on the number line. −¾ sits between 0 and −1.
Find the two integers. Cut the gap into as many equal parts as the denominator. Count from the integer closer to 0.
1½ and −1½ are the same distance from 0, on different sides. So are −0.5 and ½.
−¾ and −0.75 are equivalent. They are one point, written two ways.
The 4 in −¾ is not a place to stand. It means quarters.
journal.quote: "The denominator cuts the gap. It is NOT a floor tile." — Kwame

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 7-2 (Represent Rational Numbers and Their Opposites on the Number Line) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: placing fractions and decimals, including negatives, on the number line, opposites of rational numbers, and equivalent fraction and decimal forms.
standards: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line; extend number line diagrams to represent points with negative numbers
